[§](https://docs.rs#conditional-styling)Conditional Styling

[§](https://docs.rs#globally)Globally

Styling is enabled by default but can be enabled and disabled globally via
[ enable()](https://docs.rs/fn.enable.html) and

[. When styling is disabled, no ANSI escape codes are emitted, and](https://docs.rs/fn.disable.html)

`disable()`[values are omitted entirely.](https://docs.rs#masking)

*masked*Global styling can also be dynamically enabled and disabled using
[ whenever()](https://docs.rs/fn.whenever.html) with an arbitrary

[: a function that returns](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html)

`Condition``true` or `false`. This condition is evaluated each time a [item is displayed. The associated styling is enabled, and mask values emitted, exactly when and only when the condition returns](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html)

`Painted``true`.[§](https://docs.rs#per-style)Per-`Style`

A specific `Style` can itself be conditionally applied by using
[ .whenever()](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html#method.whenever):

```
use yansi::{Paint, Style, Color::*, Condition};
static WARNING: Style = Black.bold().on_yellow().whenever(Condition::STDERR_IS_TTY);
eprintln!("{}", "Bees can sting!".paint(WARNING));
```
With the above, if `stderr` is a TTY, then:
`>` **Bees can sting!**

If it is not a TTY, styling is not emitted:
`>` Bees can sting!

See [ Condition](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html) for a list of built-in conditions which require enabling
crate features.

[§](https://docs.rs#quirks)Quirks

As a convenience, `yansi` implements several “quirks”, applicable via
[ Quirk](https://docs.rs/enum.Quirk.html) and the respective methods, that modify if and how styling is
presented to the terminal. These quirks do not correspond to any ANSI
styling sequences.

[§](https://docs.rs#masking)Masking

Items can be arbitrarily *masked* with the [ mask()](https://docs.rs/trait.Paint.html#tymethod.mask) builder
method. Masked values are not emitted when styling is disabled, globally or
for a given style. This allows selective output based on whether styling is
enabled.

One use for this feature is to print certain characters only when styling is enabled. For instance, you might wish to emit the 🎨 emoji when coloring is enabled but not otherwise. This can be accomplished by masking the emoji:

```
use yansi::Paint;
println!("I like colors!{}", " 🎨".mask());
```
When styling is enabled, this prints: `>` I like colors! 🎨

With styling disabled, this prints: `>` I like colors!

[§](https://docs.rs#wrapping)Wrapping

**Note:** *Either the  std or alloc feature is required for wrapping.
std is enabled by default. See *

[crate features](https://docs.rs#crate-features).

Styling can *wrap* via [ Quirk::Wrap](https://docs.rs/enum.Quirk.html#variant.Wrap) or the equivalent

[constructor. A wrapping style modifies any styling resets emitted by the internal value so that they correspond to the wrapping style. In other words, the “reset” style of the wrapped item is modified to be the style being](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html#method.wrap)

`wrap()``.wrap()`d.Wrapping is useful in situations where opaque and arbitrary values must be styled consistently irrespective of any existing styling. For example, a generic logger might want to style messages based on log levels consistently, even when those messages may already include styling. Wrapping exists to enable such consistent styling:

```
use yansi::Paint;
// Imagine that `inner` is opaque and we don't know it's styling.
let inner = format!("{} and {}", "Stop".red(), "Go".green());
// We can use `wrap` to ensure anything in `inner` not styled is blue.
println!("Hey! {}", inner.blue().wrap());
```
Thanks to wrapping, this prints:
`>` Hey!
Stop and
Go

Without wrapping, the reset after `"Stop".red()` would not be overwritten:
`>` Hey! Stop and Go

Wrapping incurs a performance cost due to an extra allocation and replacement if the wrapped item has styling applied to it. Otherwise, it does not allocate nor incur a meaningful performance cost.

[§](https://docs.rs#lingering)Lingering

Styling can *linger* beyond a single value via [ Quirk::Linger](https://docs.rs/enum.Quirk.html#variant.Linger) or the
equivalent

[constructor. A lingering style does not reset itself after being applied. In other words, the style lingers on beyond the value it’s applied to, until something else resets the respective styling.](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html#method.linger)

`linger()`The complement to lingering is force resetting via [ Quirk::Resetting](https://docs.rs/enum.Quirk.html#variant.Resetting) or
the equivalent

[constructor. Force resetting, as the name implies, forces a reset suffix to be emitted after the value, irrespective of any lingering applied. It can be used as a way to finalize a lingering style.](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html#method.resetting)

`resetting()`Lingering itself is useful in situations where a given style is to be
repeated across multiple values, or when style is intended to persist even
across values that are not styled with `yansi`. It also allows avoiding
unnecessarily repeated ANSI code sequences. The examples below illustrate
some scenarios in which lingering is useful:

```
use yansi::Paint;
println!("Hello! {} {} things with {} {}?",
    "How".magenta().underline().linger(),
    "are".italic().linger(),
    "you".on_yellow(), // doesn't linger, so all styling is reset here
    "today".blue());
```
`>` Hello!
__How  are things with you__
today?

```
use yansi::Paint;
println!("Hello! {} {} things with {} {}?",
    "How".magenta().underline().linger(),
    "are".italic(), // doesn't linger, so all styling is reset here
    "you".on_yellow().linger(),
    "today".blue()); // doesn't linger; styling is reset
```
`>` Hello!
__How  are__
things with
you
today?

```
use yansi::Paint;
println!("{} B {} {} {} F",
    "A".red().linger(),
    "C".underline().linger(),
    "D", // doesn't linger, but no styling applied, thus no reset
    "E".resetting());  // explicitly reset
```
`>`  A B __C D E__  F

[§](https://docs.rs#brightening)Brightening

Most pimrary colors are available in regular and *bright* variants, e.g.,
[ Color::Red](https://docs.rs/enum.Color.html#variant.Red) and

[. The](https://docs.rs/enum.Color.html#variant.BrightRed)

`Color::BrightRed`[and](https://docs.rs/enum.Quirk.html#variant.Bright)

`Quirk::Bright`[quirks, typically applied via](https://docs.rs/enum.Quirk.html#variant.OnBright)

`Quirk::OnBright`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html#method.bright)

`.bright()`[, provide an alternative, convenient mechanism to select the bright variant of the selected foreground or background color, respectively. The quirk provides no additional colors and is equivalent to selecting the bright variants directly.](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html#method.on_bright)

`.on_bright()````
use yansi::Paint;
// These are all equivalent.
print!("{}", "Regular".red());
print!("{}", "Bright".bright_red());
print!("{}", "Bright".bright().red());
print!("{}", "Bright".red().bright());
// The `bright` quirk lets use choose the bright variants of _any_ color,
// even when the color or style is unknown at the call site.
print!("{}", "Normal".paint(STYLE));
print!("{}", "Bright".paint(STYLE).bright());
```
`>` Regular
Bright
Bright
Bright
**Normal**
**Bright**

The `bright()` quirk can be applied before or after a color is selected
while having the same effect.

[§](https://docs.rs#windows)Windows

Styling is supported and enabled automatically on Windows beginning with
the Windows 10 Anniversary Update, or about [96% of all Windows machines
worldwide](https://gs.statcounter.com/os-version-market-share/windows/desktop/worldwide),
and likely closer to 100% of developer machines (e.g., 99% of visitors to
[rocket.rs](https://rocket.rs) on Windows are on Windows 10+).

Yansi enables styling support on Windows by querying the Windows API on the first attempt to color. If support is available, it is enabled. If support is not available, styling is disabled and no styling sequences are emitted.

[§](https://docs.rs#crate-features)Crate Features

| Feature | Default? | Also Enables | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `std` | Y | `alloc` | Use `std`library. |
| `alloc` | Y | Use `alloc`. Enables[wrapping](https://docs.rs#wrapping). | |
| `detect-tty` | N | `std` | See [optional conditions](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#built-in-conditions). |
| `detect-env` | N | `std` | See [optional conditions](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#built-in-conditions). |
| `hyperlink` | N | `std` | Enables [hyperlinking](https://docs.rs/hyperlink/index.html)support. |

With `default-features = false`, this crate is `#[no_std]`.

Without any features enabled, all functionality except [wrapping](https://docs.rs#wrapping) is
available. To recover wrapping *with* `#[no_std]`, set `default-features = false` and enable the `alloc` feature, which requires `alloc` support.

One use for this feature is to print certain characters only when styling is enabled. For instance, you might wish to emit the 🎨 emoji when coloring is enabled but not otherwise. This can be accomplished by masking the emoji:

```
use yansi::Paint;
println!("I like colors!{}", " 🎨".mask());
```
When styling is enabled, this prints: `>` I like colors! 🎨

With styling disabled, this prints: `>` I like colors!

[§](https://docs.rs#wrapping)Wrapping

**Note:** *Either the  std or alloc feature is required for wrapping.
std is enabled by default. See *

[crate features](https://docs.rs#crate-features).

Styling can *wrap* via [ Quirk::Wrap](https://docs.rs/enum.Quirk.html#variant.Wrap) or the equivalent

[constructor. A wrapping style modifies any styling resets emitted by the internal value so that they correspond to the wrapping style. In other words, the “reset” style of the wrapped item is modified to be the style being](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html#method.wrap)

`wrap()``.wrap()`d.Wrapping is useful in situations where opaque and arbitrary values must be styled consistently irrespective of any existing styling. For example, a generic logger might want to style messages based on log levels consistently, even when those messages may already include styling. Wrapping exists to enable such consistent styling:

```
use yansi::Paint;
// Imagine that `inner` is opaque and we don't know it's styling.
let inner = format!("{} and {}", "Stop".red(), "Go".green());
// We can use `wrap` to ensure anything in `inner` not styled is blue.
println!("Hey! {}", inner.blue().wrap());
```
Thanks to wrapping, this prints:
`>` Hey!
Stop and
Go

Without wrapping, the reset after `"Stop".red()` would not be overwritten:
`>` Hey! Stop and Go

Wrapping incurs a performance cost due to an extra allocation and replacement if the wrapped item has styling applied to it. Otherwise, it does not allocate nor incur a meaningful performance cost.

[§](https://docs.rs#lingering)Lingering

Styling can *linger* beyond a single value via [ Quirk::Linger](https://docs.rs/enum.Quirk.html#variant.Linger) or the
equivalent

[constructor. A lingering style does not reset itself after being applied. In other words, the style lingers on beyond the value it’s applied to, until something else resets the respective styling.](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html#method.linger)

`linger()`The complement to lingering is force resetting via [ Quirk::Resetting](https://docs.rs/enum.Quirk.html#variant.Resetting) or
the equivalent

[constructor. Force resetting, as the name implies, forces a reset suffix to be emitted after the value, irrespective of any lingering applied. It can be used as a way to finalize a lingering style.](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html#method.resetting)

`resetting()`Lingering itself is useful in situations where a given style is to be
repeated across multiple values, or when style is intended to persist even
across values that are not styled with `yansi`. It also allows avoiding
unnecessarily repeated ANSI code sequences. The examples below illustrate
some scenarios in which lingering is useful:

```
use yansi::Paint;
println!("Hello! {} {} things with {} {}?",
    "How".magenta().underline().linger(),
    "are".italic().linger(),
    "you".on_yellow(), // doesn't linger, so all styling is reset here
    "today".blue());
```
`>` Hello!
__How  are things with you__
today?

```
use yansi::Paint;
println!("Hello! {} {} things with {} {}?",
    "How".magenta().underline().linger(),
    "are".italic(), // doesn't linger, so all styling is reset here
    "you".on_yellow().linger(),
    "today".blue()); // doesn't linger; styling is reset
```
`>` Hello!
__How  are__
things with
you
today?

```
use yansi::Paint;
println!("{} B {} {} {} F",
    "A".red().linger(),
    "C".underline().linger(),
    "D", // doesn't linger, but no styling applied, thus no reset
    "E".resetting());  // explicitly reset
```
`>`  A B __C D E__  F

[§](https://docs.rs#brightening)Brightening

Most pimrary colors are available in regular and *bright* variants, e.g.,
[ Color::Red](https://docs.rs/enum.Color.html#variant.Red) and

[. The](https://docs.rs/enum.Color.html#variant.BrightRed)

`Color::BrightRed`[and](https://docs.rs/enum.Quirk.html#variant.Bright)

`Quirk::Bright`[quirks, typically applied via](https://docs.rs/enum.Quirk.html#variant.OnBright)

`Quirk::OnBright`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html#method.bright)

`.bright()`[, provide an alternative, convenient mechanism to select the bright variant of the selected foreground or background color, respectively. The quirk provides no additional colors and is equivalent to selecting the bright variants directly.](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html#method.on_bright)

`.on_bright()````
use yansi::Paint;
// These are all equivalent.
print!("{}", "Regular".red());
print!("{}", "Bright".bright_red());
print!("{}", "Bright".bright().red());
print!("{}", "Bright".red().bright());
// The `bright` quirk lets use choose the bright variants of _any_ color,
// even when the color or style is unknown at the call site.
print!("{}", "Normal".paint(STYLE));
print!("{}", "Bright".paint(STYLE).bright());
```
`>` Regular
Bright
Bright
Bright
**Normal**
**Bright**

The `bright()` quirk can be applied before or after a color is selected
while having the same effect.

[§](https://docs.rs#windows)Windows

Styling is supported and enabled automatically on Windows beginning with
the Windows 10 Anniversary Update, or about [96% of all Windows machines
worldwide](https://gs.statcounter.com/os-version-market-share/windows/desktop/worldwide),
and likely closer to 100% of developer machines (e.g., 99% of visitors to
[rocket.rs](https://rocket.rs) on Windows are on Windows 10+).

Yansi enables styling support on Windows by querying the Windows API on the first attempt to color. If support is available, it is enabled. If support is not available, styling is disabled and no styling sequences are emitted.

[§](https://docs.rs#crate-features)Crate Features

| Feature | Default? | Also Enables | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `std` | Y | `alloc` | Use `std`library. |
| `alloc` | Y | Use `alloc`. Enables[wrapping](https://docs.rs#wrapping). | |
| `detect-tty` | N | `std` | See [optional conditions](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#built-in-conditions). |
| `detect-env` | N | `std` | See [optional conditions](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#built-in-conditions). |
| `hyperlink` | N | `std` | Enables [hyperlinking](https://docs.rs/hyperlink/index.html)support. |

With `default-features = false`, this crate is `#[no_std]`.

Without any features enabled, all functionality except [wrapping](https://docs.rs#wrapping) is
available. To recover wrapping *with* `#[no_std]`, set `default-features = false` and enable the `alloc` feature, which requires `alloc` support.

- [Attribute](https://docs.rs/enum.Attribute.html)

- Enum representing a `yansi`quirk.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Paint](https://docs.rs/trait.Paint.html)
- A trait to apply styling to any value. Implemented for all types.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [disable](https://docs.rs/fn.disable.html)
- Unconditionally disables styling globally.
- [enable](https://docs.rs/fn.enable.html)
- Unconditionally enables styling globally.
- [is_](https://docs.rs/fn.is_enabled.html)- enabled
- Returns `true`if styling is globally enabled and`false`otherwise.
- [whenever](https://docs.rs/fn.whenever.html)
- Dynamically enables and disables styling globally based on `condition`.

# lib.rs - source

# yansi/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! A dead simple ANSI terminal color painting library.
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//!
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! # Features
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//!
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! Why *y*et another *ANSI* terminal coloring library? Here are some reasons:
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//!
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//!   * This library makes simple things _simple_: `use` [`Paint`] and go!
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//!   * Zero dependencies by default. It really is simple.
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//!   * Zero allocations except as needed by opt-in [wrapping](#wrapping).
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//!   * [Automatic Windows support] for the vast majority (95%+) of Windows
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//!     users.
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//!   * [Featureful `no_std`], no-`alloc`, support with `default-features =
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//!     false`.
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//!   * [`Style` constructors are `const`]: store styles statically, even with
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//!     dynamic conditions!
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//!   * _Any_ type implementing a formatting trait can be styled, not just
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//!     strings.
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//!   * Styling can be [enabled] and [disabled] globally and [dynamically], on
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//!     the fly.
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//!   * A `Style` can be predicated on arbitrary [conditions](#per-style).
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//!   * Formatting specifiers like `{:x}` and `{:08b}` are supported and
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//!     preserved!
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//!   * [Built-in (optional) conditions] for [TTY detection] and [common
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//!     environment variables].
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//!   * Arbitrary items can be [_masked_] for selective disabling.
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//!   * Styling can [_wrap_] to preserve styling across resets.
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//!   * Styling can [_linger_] beyond a single value.
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//!   * Experimental support for [hyperlinking] is included.
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//!   * The name `yansi` is pretty cool 😎.
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//!
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//! All that said, `yansi` borrows API ideas from older libraries as well as
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! implementation details from [`ansi_term`].
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//!
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! [`ansi_term`]: https://crates.io/crates/ansi_term
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! [`colored`]: https://crates.io/crates/colored
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//! [`term_painter`]: https://crates.io/crates/term-painter
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! [_masked_]: #masking
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! [_wrap_]: #wrapping
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! [_linger_]: #lingering
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//! [enabled]: crate::enable
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! [disabled]: crate::disable
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//! [dynamically]: crate::whenever
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//! [enabled conditionally]: Condition
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//! [TTY detection]: Condition#impl-Condition-1
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! [common environment variables]: Condition#impl-Condition-2
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//! [Automatic Windows support]: #windows
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! [Built-in (optional) conditions]: Condition#built-in-conditions
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//! [`Style` constructors are `const`]: #uniform-const-builders
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! [hyperlinking]: hyperlink
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//! [Featureful `no_std`]: #crate-features
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//!
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//! # Usage
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//!
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//! The [`Paint`] trait is implemented for every type. Import it and call
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! chainable builder methods:
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//!
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//! ```rust
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//! use yansi::Paint;
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//!
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//! println!("Testing, {}, {}, {}!",
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//!     "Ready".bold(),
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//!     "Set".yellow().italic(),
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//!     "STOP".white().on_red().bright().underline().bold());
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! ```
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//!
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//! `>` Testing,
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//! <b>Ready</b>,
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//! <span style="color: yellow;"><i><b>Set</b></i></span>,
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//! <span style="color: white; background: red;"><u><b>STOP</b></u></span>!
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//!
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//! The methods return a [`Painted`] type which consists of a [`Style`] and a
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//! reference to the receiver. Displaying a [`Painted`] (via `print!()`,
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//! `format!()`, etc) results in emitting ANSI escape codes that effectuate the
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//! style.
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//!
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//! ## Uniform `const` Builders
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//!
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//! All builder methods are uniformly available for [`Style`], [`Color`], and
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//! [`Painted`], which means you can chain calls across library types. All
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//! methods are `const`, allowing creations of `const` or `static` [`Style`]s. A
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//! `Style` can be directly applied to values with [`.paint()`](Paint::paint()),
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//! from [`Paint::paint()`], available for every type:
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//!
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//! ```rust
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//! use yansi::{Paint, Style, Color::*};
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//!
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//! // `const` constructors allow static `Style`s for easy reuse
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//! static ALERT: Style = White.bright().underline().italic().on_red();
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//!
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//! println!("Testing, {}, {}, {}!",
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//!     "Ready".bold(),
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//!     "Set".yellow().bold(),
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//!     "STOP".paint(ALERT));
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//! ```
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//!
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//! `>` Testing,
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//! <b>Ready</b>,
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//! <span style="color: yellow;"><b>Set</b></span>,
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//! <span style="color: white; background: red;"><u><em>STOP</em></u></span>!
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//!
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//! ## Conditional Styling
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//!
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//! ### Globally
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//!
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//! Styling is enabled by default but can be enabled and disabled globally via
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//! [`enable()`] and [`disable()`]. When styling is disabled, no ANSI escape
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//! codes are emitted, and [_masked_] values are omitted entirely.
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//!
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//! Global styling can also be dynamically enabled and disabled using
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//! [`whenever()`] with an arbitrary [`Condition`]: a function that returns
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//! `true` or `false`. This condition is evaluated each time a [`Painted`] item
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//! is displayed. The associated styling is enabled, and mask values emitted,
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//! exactly when and only when the condition returns `true`.
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//!
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//! ### Per-`Style`
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//!
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//! A specific `Style` can itself be conditionally applied by using
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//! [`.whenever()`](Style::whenever()):
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//!
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//! ```rust
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//! # #[cfg(feature = "detect-tty")] {
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//! use yansi::{Paint, Style, Color::*, Condition};
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//!
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//! static WARNING: Style = Black.bold().on_yellow().whenever(Condition::STDERR_IS_TTY);
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//!
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//! eprintln!("{}", "Bees can sting!".paint(WARNING));
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//! # }
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//! ```
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//!
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//! With the above, if `stderr` is a TTY, then:
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//! `>` <span style="background: yellow; color: black;"><b>Bees can sting!</b></span>
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//!
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//! If it is not a TTY, styling is not emitted:
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//! `>` Bees can sting!
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//!
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//! See [`Condition`] for a list of built-in conditions which require enabling
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//! crate features.
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//!
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//! # Quirks
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//!
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//! As a convenience, `yansi` implements several "quirks", applicable via
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//! [`Quirk`] and the respective methods, that modify if and how styling is
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//! presented to the terminal. These quirks do not correspond to any ANSI
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//! styling sequences.
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//!
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//! ## Masking
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//!
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//! Items can be arbitrarily _masked_ with the [`mask()`](Paint::mask()) builder
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//! method. Masked values are not emitted when styling is disabled, globally or
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//! for a given style. This allows selective output based on whether styling is
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//! enabled.
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//!
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//! One use for this feature is to print certain characters only when styling is
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//! enabled. For instance, you might wish to emit the 🎨 emoji when coloring is
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//! enabled but not otherwise. This can be accomplished by masking the emoji:
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//!
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//! ```rust
[158](https://docs.rs#158)//! use yansi::Paint;
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//!
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//! println!("I like colors!{}", " 🎨".mask());
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//! ```
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//!
[163](https://docs.rs#163)//! When styling is enabled, this prints: `>` I like colors! 🎨
[164](https://docs.rs#164)//!
[165](https://docs.rs#165)//! With styling disabled, this prints: `>` I like colors!
[166](https://docs.rs#166)//!
[167](https://docs.rs#167)//! ## Wrapping
[168](https://docs.rs#168)//!
[169](https://docs.rs#169)//! **Note:** _Either the `std` or `alloc` feature is required for wrapping.
[170](https://docs.rs#170)//! `std` is enabled by default. See [crate features](#crate-features)._
[171](https://docs.rs#171)//!
[172](https://docs.rs#172)//! Styling can _wrap_ via [`Quirk::Wrap`] or the equivalent
[173](https://docs.rs#173)//! [`wrap()`](Painted::wrap()) constructor. A wrapping style modifies any
[174](https://docs.rs#174)//! styling resets emitted by the internal value so that they correspond to the
[175](https://docs.rs#175)//! wrapping style. In other words, the "reset" style of the wrapped item is
[176](https://docs.rs#176)//! modified to be the style being `.wrap()`d.
[177](https://docs.rs#177)//!
[178](https://docs.rs#178)//! Wrapping is useful in situations where opaque and arbitrary values must be
[179](https://docs.rs#179)//! styled consistently irrespective of any existing styling. For example, a
[180](https://docs.rs#180)//! generic logger might want to style messages based on log levels
[181](https://docs.rs#181)//! consistently, even when those messages may already include styling. Wrapping
[182](https://docs.rs#182)//! exists to enable such consistent styling:
[183](https://docs.rs#183)//!
[184](https://docs.rs#184)//! ```rust
[185](https://docs.rs#185)//! use yansi::Paint;
[186](https://docs.rs#186)//!
[187](https://docs.rs#187)//! // Imagine that `inner` is opaque and we don't know it's styling.
[188](https://docs.rs#188)//! let inner = format!("{} and {}", "Stop".red(), "Go".green());
[189](https://docs.rs#189)//!
[190](https://docs.rs#190)//! // We can use `wrap` to ensure anything in `inner` not styled is blue.
[191](https://docs.rs#191)//! println!("Hey! {}", inner.blue().wrap());
[192](https://docs.rs#192)//! ```
[193](https://docs.rs#193)//!
[194](https://docs.rs#194)//! Thanks to wrapping, this prints:
[195](https://docs.rs#195)//! `>` Hey! <span style="color: blue">
[196](https://docs.rs#196)//! <span style="color: red">Stop</span> and
[197](https://docs.rs#197)//! <span style="color: green">Go</span>
[198](https://docs.rs#198)//! </span>
[199](https://docs.rs#199)//!
[200](https://docs.rs#200)//! Without wrapping, the reset after `"Stop".red()` would not be overwritten:
[201](https://docs.rs#201)//! `>` Hey! <span style="color: red">Stop</span> and <span style="color: green">Go</span>
[202](https://docs.rs#202)//!
[203](https://docs.rs#203)//! Wrapping incurs a performance cost due to an extra allocation and
[204](https://docs.rs#204)//! replacement if the wrapped item has styling applied to it. Otherwise, it
[205](https://docs.rs#205)//! does not allocate nor incur a meaningful performance cost.
[206](https://docs.rs#206)//!
[207](https://docs.rs#207)//! ## Lingering
[208](https://docs.rs#208)//!
[209](https://docs.rs#209)//! Styling can _linger_ beyond a single value via [`Quirk::Linger`] or the
[210](https://docs.rs#210)//! equivalent [`linger()`](Painted::linger()) constructor. A lingering style
[211](https://docs.rs#211)//! does not reset itself after being applied. In other words, the style lingers
[212](https://docs.rs#212)//! on beyond the value it's applied to, until something else resets the
[213](https://docs.rs#213)//! respective styling.
[214](https://docs.rs#214)//!
[215](https://docs.rs#215)//! The complement to lingering is force resetting via [`Quirk::Resetting`] or
[216](https://docs.rs#216)//! the equivalent [`resetting()`](Painted::resetting()) constructor. Force
[217](https://docs.rs#217)//! resetting, as the name implies, forces a reset suffix to be emitted after
[218](https://docs.rs#218)//! the value, irrespective of any lingering applied. It can be used as a way to
[219](https://docs.rs#219)//! finalize a lingering style.
[220](https://docs.rs#220)//!
[221](https://docs.rs#221)//! Lingering itself is useful in situations where a given style is to be
[222](https://docs.rs#222)//! repeated across multiple values, or when style is intended to persist even
[223](https://docs.rs#223)//! across values that are not styled with `yansi`. It also allows avoiding
[224](https://docs.rs#224)//! unnecessarily repeated ANSI code sequences. The examples below illustrate
[225](https://docs.rs#225)//! some scenarios in which lingering is useful:
[226](https://docs.rs#226)//!
[227](https://docs.rs#227)//! ```rust
[228](https://docs.rs#228)//! use yansi::Paint;
[229](https://docs.rs#229)//!
[230](https://docs.rs#230)//! println!("Hello! {} {} things with {} {}?",
[231](https://docs.rs#231)//!     "How".magenta().underline().linger(),
[232](https://docs.rs#232)//!     "are".italic().linger(),
[233](https://docs.rs#233)//!     "you".on_yellow(), // doesn't linger, so all styling is reset here
[234](https://docs.rs#234)//!     "today".blue());
[235](https://docs.rs#235)//! ```
[236](https://docs.rs#236)//!
[237](https://docs.rs#237)//! `>` Hello!
[238](https://docs.rs#238)//! <span style="color: magenta;">
[239](https://docs.rs#239)//!   <u>How <i>are things with <span style="background: yellow;">you</span></i></u>
[240](https://docs.rs#240)//! </span>

[242](https://docs.rs#242)//!

[244](https://docs.rs#244)//! use yansi::Paint;
[245](https://docs.rs#245)//!
[246](https://docs.rs#246)//! println!("Hello! {} {} things with {} {}?",
[247](https://docs.rs#247)//!     "How".magenta().underline().linger(),
[248](https://docs.rs#248)//!     "are".italic(), // doesn't linger, so all styling is reset here
[249](https://docs.rs#249)//!     "you".on_yellow().linger(),
[250](https://docs.rs#250)//!     "today".blue()); // doesn't linger; styling is reset
[251](https://docs.rs#251)//! ```
[252](https://docs.rs#252)//!
[253](https://docs.rs#253)//! `>` Hello!
[254](https://docs.rs#254)//! <span style="color: magenta;">
[255](https://docs.rs#255)//!   <u>How <i>are</i></u>
[256](https://docs.rs#256)//! </span>
[257](https://docs.rs#257)//! things with
[258](https://docs.rs#258)//! <span style="background: yellow;">
[259](https://docs.rs#259)//! you
[260](https://docs.rs#260)//! <span style="color: blue;">today</span></span>?
[261](https://docs.rs#261)//!
[262](https://docs.rs#262)//! ```rust
[263](https://docs.rs#263)//! use yansi::Paint;
[264](https://docs.rs#264)//!
[265](https://docs.rs#265)//! println!("{} B {} {} {} F",
[266](https://docs.rs#266)//!     "A".red().linger(),
[267](https://docs.rs#267)//!     "C".underline().linger(),
[268](https://docs.rs#268)//!     "D", // doesn't linger, but no styling applied, thus no reset
[269](https://docs.rs#269)//!     "E".resetting());  // explicitly reset
[270](https://docs.rs#270)//! ```
[271](https://docs.rs#271)//!
[272](https://docs.rs#272)//! `>` <span style="color: red;"> A B <u>C D E</u> </span> F
[273](https://docs.rs#273)//!
[274](https://docs.rs#274)//! ## Brightening
[275](https://docs.rs#275)//!
[276](https://docs.rs#276)//! Most pimrary colors are available in regular and _bright_ variants, e.g.,
[277](https://docs.rs#277)//! [`Color::Red`] and [`Color::BrightRed`]. The [`Quirk::Bright`] and
[278](https://docs.rs#278)//! [`Quirk::OnBright`] quirks, typically applied via
[279](https://docs.rs#279)//! [`.bright()`](Painted::bright()) and [`.on_bright()`](Painted::on_bright()),
[280](https://docs.rs#280)//! provide an alternative, convenient mechanism to select the bright variant of
[281](https://docs.rs#281)//! the selected foreground or background color, respectively. The quirk
[282](https://docs.rs#282)//! provides no additional colors and is equivalent to selecting the bright
[283](https://docs.rs#283)//! variants directly.
[284](https://docs.rs#284)//!
[285](https://docs.rs#285)//! ```rust
[286](https://docs.rs#286)//! use yansi::Paint;
[287](https://docs.rs#287)//!
[288](https://docs.rs#288)//! // These are all equivalent.
[289](https://docs.rs#289)//! print!("{}", "Regular".red());
[290](https://docs.rs#290)//! print!("{}", "Bright".bright_red());
[291](https://docs.rs#291)//! print!("{}", "Bright".bright().red());
[292](https://docs.rs#292)//! print!("{}", "Bright".red().bright());
[293](https://docs.rs#293)//!
[294](https://docs.rs#294)//! # static STYLE: yansi::Style = yansi::Color::Green.bold();
[295](https://docs.rs#295)//! // The `bright` quirk lets use choose the bright variants of _any_ color,
[296](https://docs.rs#296)//! // even when the color or style is unknown at the call site.
[297](https://docs.rs#297)//! print!("{}", "Normal".paint(STYLE));
[298](https://docs.rs#298)//! print!("{}", "Bright".paint(STYLE).bright());
[299](https://docs.rs#299)//! ```
[300](https://docs.rs#300)//!
[301](https://docs.rs#301)//! `>` <span style="color: red;">Regular</span>
[302](https://docs.rs#302)//! <span style="color: hotpink;">Bright</span>
[303](https://docs.rs#303)//! <span style="color: hotpink;">Bright</span>
[304](https://docs.rs#304)//! <span style="color: hotpink;">Bright</span>
[305](https://docs.rs#305)//! <span style="color: green;"><b>Normal</b></span>
[306](https://docs.rs#306)//! <span style="color: greenyellow;"><b>Bright</b></span>
[307](https://docs.rs#307)//!
[308](https://docs.rs#308)//! The `bright()` quirk can be applied before or after a color is selected
[309](https://docs.rs#309)//! while having the same effect.
[310](https://docs.rs#310)//!
[311](https://docs.rs#311)//! # Windows
[312](https://docs.rs#312)//!
[313](https://docs.rs#313)//! Styling is supported and enabled automatically on Windows beginning with
[314](https://docs.rs#314)//! the Windows 10 Anniversary Update, or about [96% of all Windows machines
[315](https://docs.rs#315)//! worldwide](https://gs.statcounter.com/os-version-market-share/windows/desktop/worldwide),
[316](https://docs.rs#316)//! and likely closer to 100% of developer machines (e.g., 99% of visitors to
[317](https://docs.rs#317)//! [rocket.rs](https://rocket.rs) on Windows are on Windows 10+).
[318](https://docs.rs#318)//!
[319](https://docs.rs#319)//! Yansi enables styling support on Windows by querying the Windows API on the
[320](https://docs.rs#320)//! first attempt to color. If support is available, it is enabled. If support
[321](https://docs.rs#321)//! is not available, styling is disabled and no styling sequences are emitted.

}## Expand description

A trait to apply styling to any value. Implemented for all types.

Because this trait is implemented for all types, you can use its methods on
any type. With the exception of one constructor method, [ Paint::new()](https://docs.rs/trait.Paint.html#method.new),
all methods are called with method syntax:

```
use yansi::Paint;
"hello".green(); // calls `Paint::<&'static str>::green()`.
"hello".strike(); // calls `Paint::<&'static str>::strike()`.
1.on_red(); // calls `Paint::<i32>::red()`.
1.blink(); // calls `Paint::<i32>::blink()`.
```
[§](https://docs.rs#chaining)Chaining

All methods return a [ Painted](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html) whose methods are exactly those of

`Paint`.
This means you can chain `Paint` method calls:```
use yansi::Paint;
"hello".green().strike(); // calls `Paint::green()` then `Painted::strike()`.
1.on_red().blink(); // calls `Paint::red()` + `Painted::blink()`.
```
[§](https://docs.rs#borrow-vs-owned-receiver)Borrow vs. Owned Receiver

The returned [ Painted](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html) type contains a borrow to the receiver:

```
use yansi::{Paint, Painted};
let v: Painted<&i32> = 1.red();
```
This is nearly always what you want. In the exceedingly rare case that you
*do* want `Painted` to own its value, use [ Paint::new()](https://docs.rs/trait.Paint.html#method.new) or the equivalent

[:](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html#method.new)

`Painted::new()````
use yansi::{Paint, Painted};
let v: Painted<i32> = Paint::new(1);
let v: Painted<i32> = Painted::new(1);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#further-details)Further Details

See the [crate level docs](https://docs.rs/index.html#usage) for more details and examples.

Returns a styled value derived from `self` with the foreground set to
`value`.

This method should be used rarely. Instead, prefer to use color-specific
builder methods like [ red()](https://docs.rs/trait.Paint.html#tymethod.red) and

[, which have the same functionality but are pithier.](https://docs.rs/trait.Paint.html#tymethod.green)

# enable in yansi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yansi/1.0.1/yansi/fn.enable.html

`pub fn enable()`## Expand description

Unconditionally enables styling globally.

By default, styling is enabled based on [ Condition::DEFAULT](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#associatedconstant.DEFAULT), which checks
for operating system support.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use yansi::Paint;
// With styling disabled, ANSI color codes are _not_ emitted.
yansi::disable();
assert_eq!("go".green().to_string(), "go".to_string());
// Reenabling causes color code to be emitted.
yansi::enable();
assert_ne!("go".green().to_string(), "go".to_string());
```

# disable in yansi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yansi/1.0.1/yansi/fn.disable.html

`pub fn disable()`## Expand description

Unconditionally disables styling globally.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use yansi::Paint;
// With styling enabled, ANSI color codes are emitted, thus `ne`.
assert_ne!("go".green().to_string(), "go".to_string());
// With styling disabled, ANSI color codes are _not_ emitted.
yansi::disable();
assert_eq!("go".green().to_string(), "go".to_string());
```

# whenever in yansi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yansi/1.0.1/yansi/fn.whenever.html

`pub fn whenever(condition: `[Condition](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html))## Expand description

Dynamically enables and disables styling globally based on `condition`.

`condition` is expected to be fast: it is checked dynamically, each time a
[ Painted](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html) value is displayed.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use yansi::Condition;
yansi::whenever(Condition::STDOUT_IS_TTY);
// On each styling, check if we have TTYs.
yansi::whenever(Condition::STDOUTERR_ARE_TTY_LIVE);
// Check `NO_COLOR`, `CLICOLOR`, and if we have TTYs.
const HAVE_COLOR: Condition = Condition(|| {
    std::env::var_os("NO_COLOR").is_none()
        && (Condition::CLICOLOR_LIVE)()
        && Condition::stdouterr_are_tty_live()
});
// This will call `HAVE_COLOR` every time styling is needed. In this
// example, this means that env vars will be checked on each styling.
yansi::whenever(HAVE_COLOR);
// This instead caches the value (checking `env()` exactly once, now).
yansi::whenever(Condition::cached((HAVE_COLOR)()));
// Is identical to this:
match (HAVE_COLOR)() {
    true => yansi::enable(),
    false => yansi::disable(),
}
```

# Condition in yansi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yansi/1.0.1/yansi/struct.Condition.html

## Expand description

A function that decides whether styling should be applied.

A styling `Condition` can be specified globally via
[ yansi::whenever()](https://docs.rs/fn.whenever.html) or locally to a specific style via
the

[builder method. Any time a](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html#method.whenever)

`whenever()`[value is formatted, both the local and global conditions are checked, and only when both evaluate to](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html)

`Painted``true` is styling
actually applied.A `Condition` is nothing more than a function that returns a `bool`. The
function is called each and every time a `Painted` is formatted, and so it
is expected to be fast. All of the built-in conditions (except for their
“live” variants) cache their first evaluation as a result: the
[ Condition::cached()](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#method.cached) constructor can do the same for your conditions.

[§](https://docs.rs#built-in-conditions)Built-In Conditions

`yansi` comes with built-in conditions for common scenarios that can be
enabled via crate features:

| feature(s) | condition | implication |
|---|---|---|
| `detect-tty` | [TTY Detectors](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#impl-Condition-1) | `std`,`is-terminal` |
| `detect-env` | [Environment Variable Checkers](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#impl-Condition-2) | `std` |
| [ `detect-tty`,`detect-env`] | All Above, [Combo Detectors](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#impl-Condition-3) | `std`,`is-terminal` |

For example, to enable the TTY detectors, enable the `detect-tty` feature:

`yansi = { version = "...", features = ["detect-tty"] }`To enable the TTY detectors, env-var checkers, and combo detectors, enable
`detect-tty` *and* `detect-env`:

`yansi = { version = "...", features = ["detect-tty", "detect-env"] }````
use yansi::Condition;
yansi::whenever(Condition::TTY_AND_COLOR);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#custom-conditions)Custom Conditions

Custom, arbitrary conditions can be created with [ Condition::from()](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#method.from) or

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#method.cached)

`Condition::cached()````
use yansi::{Condition, Style, Color::*};
// Combine two conditions (`stderr` is a TTY, `CLICOLOR` is set) into one.
static STDERR_COLOR: Condition = Condition::from(||
    Condition::stderr_is_tty() && Condition::clicolor()
);
static DEBUG: Style = Yellow.bold().on_primary().invert().whenever(STDERR_COLOR);
```

The function `f` is called anytime the condition is checked, including
every time a style with the condition is used.

// Create a condition on the stack from a function.
let my_condition = Condition::from(some_function);
// Create a static condition from a closure that becomes a `fn`.

// Create a condition on the stack from a closure that becomes a `fn`.
let my_condition = Condition::from(|| some_function());
```

# yansi::hyperlink - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yansi/1.0.1/yansi/hyperlink/index.html

**crate feature**only.

`hyperlink`## Expand description

Experimental support for hyperlinking.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Enable the `hyperlink` crate feature. Enabling `hyperlink` implicitly
enables `std`.

Import the `HyperlinkExt` extension trait and use the [ link()](https://docs.rs/trait.HyperlinkExt.html#tymethod.link) builder
method.

```
use yansi::Paint;
use yansi::hyperlink::HyperlinkExt;
println!("Go to {}.", "our docs".link("https://docs.rs/yansi").green());
```
`>` Go to [our docs](https://docs.rs/yansi).

The `link()` method returns a [ PaintedLink](https://docs.rs/struct.PaintedLink.html) structure which implements all
of the unverisal chainable methods available across the library.
Furthermore,

[is extended with a](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html)

`Painted`[method. The net effect is that you can use](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html#method.link)

`link()``link()` as if it were any other
styling method:```
use yansi::Paint;
use yansi::hyperlink::HyperlinkExt;
println!("Go to {}.", "our docs".green().link("https://docs.rs/yansi").on_black().invert());
```
`>` Go to [
our docs
](https://docs.rs/yansi).

[§](https://docs.rs#caveats)Caveats

-
You can only create a link when there is a target value to print, that is, when the receiver is something “printable”. In other words, you *cannot*apply`link()`to a bare`Style`. This means the following will not work:[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)`use yansi::{Paint, Style, Color::*}; use yansi::hyperlink::HyperlinkExt; static LINKED: Style = Green.link("https://docs.rs/yansi");`

-
While some modern terminals support hyperlinking, many do not. Those that do not *should*gracefully ignore the target URL and print the original value. That is, instead of`>`[our docs](https://docs.rs/yansi), such terminals would print`>`our docs.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Painted](https://docs.rs/struct.PaintedLink.html)- Link
- A `Painted`

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Hyperlink](https://docs.rs/trait.HyperlinkExt.html)- Ext
- Extension trait to apply hyperlinks to any value, implemented for all types.

}Expand description A set of styling options.

§ Equivalence and OrderingOnly a style’s `foreground`, `background`, and set of `attributes` are
considered when testing for equivalence or producing an ordering via
`PartialEq` or `Eq`, and `PartialOrd` or `Ord`. A style’s quirks and
conditions are ignored.

The foreground color. Defaults to `None`.

use  yansi::{Style, Color};
assert_eq! (Style::new().foreground, None );
assert_eq! (Style::new().green().foreground, Some (Color::Green));The background color. Defaults to `None`.

use  yansi::{Style, Color};
assert_eq! (Style::new().background, None );
assert_eq! (Style::new().on_red().background, Some (Color::Red));The condition.

To check a style’s condition directly, use `Style::enabled()`

use  yansi::{Style, Condition};
let  style = Style::new().whenever(Condition::ALWAYS);
assert! (style.enabled());
let  style = Style::new().whenever(Condition::NEVER);
assert! (!style.enabled());Returns a new style with no foreground or background, no attributes
or quirks, and `Condition::DEFAULT`

This is the default returned by `Default::default()`

§ Exampleuse  yansi::Style;
assert_eq! (Style::new(), Style::default());Returns `true` if this style is enabled, based on
`condition`

Note:  For a style to be effected, both this method and
`yansi::is_enabled()``true`.

When there is no condition set, this method always returns `true`. When
a condition has been set, this evaluates the condition and returns the
result.

This method writes the ANSI code prefix irrespective of whether painting
is currently enabled or disabled. To write the prefix only if painting

§ Exampleuse  core::fmt;
use  yansi::Style;

impl  fmt::Display for  CustomItem {
    fn  fmt(& self , f: &mut  fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
        self .style.fmt_prefix(f)? ;
        write! (f, "number: {}" , self .item)? ;
        self .style.fmt_suffix(f)
    }

Expand description Enum representing a terminal color.

Note:  The color examples below are purely demonstrative. The actual
color rendered depends entirely on the terminal and its configuration, the
latter of which is entirely arbitrary.

Terminal primary color #9. (foreground code `39`, background code `49`).

This is the terminal’s defined “primary” color, that is, the configured
default foreground and background colors. As such, this color as a
foreground looks “good” against the terminal’s default background color,
and this color is a “good” background color for the terminal’s default
foreground color.

A color from 0 to 255, for use in 256-color terminals.

# Attribute in yansi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yansi/1.0.1/yansi/enum.Attribute.html

Enum Attribute  Copy item path  Source  ```
pub enum Attribute {
    Bold,
    Dim,
    Italic,
    Underline,
    Blink,
    RapidBlink,
    Invert,
    Conceal,
    Strike,
}
```
Expand description Enum representing text attributes, largely for text formatting.

Text attributes are typically applied to a `Style``Color``Painted``bold()``italic()`

Attributes are idempotent, so applying an attribute more than once has no
more affect than applying it once.

§ Terminal SupportWhether an applied attribute actually has an effect on how text is rendered
in a terminal depends on the terminal’s support for the attribute as well as
the terminal’s configuration. Common attributes, such as `bold`, `dim`,
`italic`, `underline`, and `strike` typically have good support and are
largely reliable. Less commonly supported attributes like `conceal` and
`invert` will usually  be supported by “modern” terminals. Rarely supported
attributes, such as  `blink` and `rapid blink`, will typically have no
effect when applied.

# is_enabled in yansi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yansi/1.0.1/yansi/fn.is_enabled.html

`pub fn is_enabled() -> `[bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)## Expand description

Returns `true` if styling is globally enabled and `false` otherwise.

By default, styling is enabled based on [ Condition::DEFAULT](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#associatedconstant.DEFAULT), which checks
for operating system support. It can be enabled and disabled on-the-fly with

[and](https://docs.rs/fn.enable.html)

`enable()`[and via a dynamic condition with](https://docs.rs/fn.disable.html)

`disable()`[.](https://docs.rs/fn.whenever.html)

`whenever()`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
// Styling is enabled by default.
assert!(yansi::is_enabled());
// Disable it with `Painted::disable()`.
yansi::disable();
assert!(!yansi::is_enabled());
// Reenable with `Painted::enable()`.
yansi::enable();
assert!(yansi::is_enabled());
```

# yansi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yansi/latest/yansi/

## Expand description

A dead simple ANSI terminal color painting library.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

Why *y*et another *ANSI* terminal coloring library? Here are some reasons:

- This library makes simple things *simple*:`use``Paint`
- Zero dependencies by default. It really is simple.
- Zero allocations except as needed by opt-in [wrapping](https://docs.rs#wrapping).
- [Automatic Windows support](https://docs.rs#windows)for the vast majority (95%+) of Windows users.
- [Featureful](https://docs.rs#crate-features), no-- `no_std`- `alloc`, support with- `default-features = false`.
- `Style`constructors are- `const`
- *Any*type implementing a formatting trait can be styled, not just strings.
- Styling can be [enabled](https://docs.rs/fn.enable.html)and[disabled](https://docs.rs/fn.disable.html)globally and[dynamically](https://docs.rs/fn.whenever.html), on the fly.
- A `Style`can be predicated on arbitrary[conditions](https://docs.rs#per-style).
- Formatting specifiers like `{:x}`and`{:08b}`are supported and preserved!
- [Built-in (optional) conditions](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#built-in-conditions)for- [TTY detection](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#impl-Condition-1)and- [common environment variables](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#impl-Condition-2).
- Arbitrary items can be *masked*
- Styling can *wrap*
- Styling can *linger*
- Experimental support for [hyperlinking](https://docs.rs/hyperlink/index.html)is included.
- The name `yansi`is pretty cool 😎.

All that said, `yansi` borrows API ideas from older libraries as well as
implementation details from [ ansi_term](https://crates.io/crates/ansi_term).

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The [ Paint](https://docs.rs/trait.Paint.html) trait is implemented for every type. Import it and call
chainable builder methods:

```
use yansi::Paint;
println!("Testing, {}, {}, {}!",
    "Ready".bold(),
    "Set".yellow().italic(),
    "STOP".white().on_red().bright().underline().bold());
```
`>` Testing,
**Ready**,
* Set*,

__!__

**STOP**The methods return a [ Painted](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html) type which consists of a

[and a reference to the receiver. Displaying a](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html)

`Style`[(via](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html)

`Painted``print!()`,
`format!()`, etc) results in emitting ANSI escape codes that effectuate the
style.[§](https://docs.rs#uniform-const-builders)Uniform `const` Builders

All builder methods are uniformly available for [ Style](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html),

[, and](https://docs.rs/enum.Color.html)

`Color`[, which means you can chain calls across library types. All methods are](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html)

`Painted``const`, allowing creations of `const` or `static` [s. A](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html)

`Style``Style` can be directly applied to values with [, from](https://docs.rs/trait.Paint.html#method.paint)

`.paint()`[, available for every type:](https://docs.rs/trait.Paint.html#method.paint)

`Paint::paint()````
use yansi::{Paint, Style, Color::*};
// `const` constructors allow static `Style`s for easy reuse
static ALERT: Style = White.bright().underline().italic().on_red();
println!("Testing, {}, {}, {}!",
    "Ready".bold(),
    "Set".yellow().bold(),
    "STOP".paint(ALERT));
```
`>` Testing,
**Ready**,
**Set**,
__ STOP__!

[§](https://docs.rs#conditional-styling)Conditional Styling

[§](https://docs.rs#globally)Globally

Styling is enabled by default but can be enabled and disabled globally via
[ enable()](https://docs.rs/fn.enable.html) and

[. When styling is disabled, no ANSI escape codes are emitted, and](https://docs.rs/fn.disable.html)

`disable()`[values are omitted entirely.](https://docs.rs#masking)

*masked*Global styling can also be dynamically enabled and disabled using
[ whenever()](https://docs.rs/fn.whenever.html) with an arbitrary

[: a function that returns](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html)

`Condition``true` or `false`. This condition is evaluated each time a [item is displayed. The associated styling is enabled, and mask values emitted, exactly when and only when the condition returns](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html)

`Painted``true`.[§](https://docs.rs#per-style)Per-`Style`

A specific `Style` can itself be conditionally applied by using
[ .whenever()](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html#method.whenever):

```
use yansi::{Paint, Style, Color::*, Condition};
static WARNING: Style = Black.bold().on_yellow().whenever(Condition::STDERR_IS_TTY);
eprintln!("{}", "Bees can sting!".paint(WARNING));
```
With the above, if `stderr` is a TTY, then:
`>` **Bees can sting!**

If it is not a TTY, styling is not emitted:
`>` Bees can sting!

See [ Condition](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html) for a list of built-in conditions which require enabling
crate features.

[§](https://docs.rs#quirks)Quirks

As a convenience, `yansi` implements several “quirks”, applicable via
[ Quirk](https://docs.rs/enum.Quirk.html) and the respective methods, that modify if and how styling is
presented to the terminal. These quirks do not correspond to any ANSI
styling sequences.

[§](https://docs.rs#masking)Masking

Items can be arbitrarily *masked* with the [ mask()](https://docs.rs/trait.Paint.html#tymethod.mask) builder
method. Masked values are not emitted when styling is disabled, globally or
for a given style. This allows selective output based on whether styling is
enabled.

One use for this feature is to print certain characters only when styling is enabled. For instance, you might wish to emit the 🎨 emoji when coloring is enabled but not otherwise. This can be accomplished by masking the emoji:

```
use yansi::Paint;
println!("I like colors!{}", " 🎨".mask());
```
When styling is enabled, this prints: `>` I like colors! 🎨

With styling disabled, this prints: `>` I like colors!

[§](https://docs.rs#wrapping)Wrapping

**Note:** *Either the  std or alloc feature is required for wrapping.
std is enabled by default. See *

[crate features](https://docs.rs#crate-features).

Styling can *wrap* via [ Quirk::Wrap](https://docs.rs/enum.Quirk.html#variant.Wrap) or the equivalent

[constructor. A wrapping style modifies any styling resets emitted by the internal value so that they correspond to the wrapping style. In other words, the “reset” style of the wrapped item is modified to be the style being](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html#method.wrap)

`wrap()``.wrap()`d.Wrapping is useful in situations where opaque and arbitrary values must be styled consistently irrespective of any existing styling. For example, a generic logger might want to style messages based on log levels consistently, even when those messages may already include styling. Wrapping exists to enable such consistent styling:

```
use yansi::Paint;
// Imagine that `inner` is opaque and we don't know it's styling.
let inner = format!("{} and {}", "Stop".red(), "Go".green());
// We can use `wrap` to ensure anything in `inner` not styled is blue.
println!("Hey! {}", inner.blue().wrap());
```
Thanks to wrapping, this prints:
`>` Hey!
Stop and
Go

Without wrapping, the reset after `"Stop".red()` would not be overwritten:
`>` Hey! Stop and Go

Wrapping incurs a performance cost due to an extra allocation and replacement if the wrapped item has styling applied to it. Otherwise, it does not allocate nor incur a meaningful performance cost.

[§](https://docs.rs#lingering)Lingering

Styling can *linger* beyond a single value via [ Quirk::Linger](https://docs.rs/enum.Quirk.html#variant.Linger) or the
equivalent

[constructor. A lingering style does not reset itself after being applied. In other words, the style lingers on beyond the value it’s applied to, until something else resets the respective styling.](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html#method.linger)

`linger()`The complement to lingering is force resetting via [ Quirk::Resetting](https://docs.rs/enum.Quirk.html#variant.Resetting) or
the equivalent

[constructor. Force resetting, as the name implies, forces a reset suffix to be emitted after the value, irrespective of any lingering applied. It can be used as a way to finalize a lingering style.](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html#method.resetting)

`resetting()`Lingering itself is useful in situations where a given style is to be
repeated across multiple values, or when style is intended to persist even
across values that are not styled with `yansi`. It also allows avoiding
unnecessarily repeated ANSI code sequences. The examples below illustrate
some scenarios in which lingering is useful:

```
use yansi::Paint;
println!("Hello! {} {} things with {} {}?",
    "How".magenta().underline().linger(),
    "are".italic().linger(),
    "you".on_yellow(), // doesn't linger, so all styling is reset here
    "today".blue());
```
`>` Hello!
__How  are things with you__
today?

```
use yansi::Paint;
println!("Hello! {} {} things with {} {}?",
    "How".magenta().underline().linger(),
    "are".italic(), // doesn't linger, so all styling is reset here
    "you".on_yellow().linger(),
    "today".blue()); // doesn't linger; styling is reset
```
`>` Hello!
__How  are__
things with
you
today?

```
use yansi::Paint;
println!("{} B {} {} {} F",
    "A".red().linger(),
    "C".underline().linger(),
    "D", // doesn't linger, but no styling applied, thus no reset
    "E".resetting());  // explicitly reset
```
`>`  A B __C D E__  F

[§](https://docs.rs#brightening)Brightening

Most pimrary colors are available in regular and *bright* variants, e.g.,
[ Color::Red](https://docs.rs/enum.Color.html#variant.Red) and

[. The](https://docs.rs/enum.Color.html#variant.BrightRed)

`Color::BrightRed`[and](https://docs.rs/enum.Quirk.html#variant.Bright)

`Quirk::Bright`[quirks, typically applied via](https://docs.rs/enum.Quirk.html#variant.OnBright)

`Quirk::OnBright`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html#method.bright)

`.bright()`[, provide an alternative, convenient mechanism to select the bright variant of the selected foreground or background color, respectively. The quirk provides no additional colors and is equivalent to selecting the bright variants directly.](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html#method.on_bright)

`.on_bright()````
use yansi::Paint;
// These are all equivalent.
print!("{}", "Regular".red());
print!("{}", "Bright".bright_red());
print!("{}", "Bright".bright().red());
print!("{}", "Bright".red().bright());
// The `bright` quirk lets use choose the bright variants of _any_ color,
// even when the color or style is unknown at the call site.
print!("{}", "Normal".paint(STYLE));
print!("{}", "Bright".paint(STYLE).bright());
```
`>` Regular
Bright
Bright
Bright
**Normal**
**Bright**

The `bright()` quirk can be applied before or after a color is selected
while having the same effect.

[§](https://docs.rs#windows)Windows

Styling is supported and enabled automatically on Windows beginning with
the Windows 10 Anniversary Update, or about [96% of all Windows machines
worldwide](https://gs.statcounter.com/os-version-market-share/windows/desktop/worldwide),
and likely closer to 100% of developer machines (e.g., 99% of visitors to
[rocket.rs](https://rocket.rs) on Windows are on Windows 10+).

Yansi enables styling support on Windows by querying the Windows API on the first attempt to color. If support is available, it is enabled. If support is not available, styling is disabled and no styling sequences are emitted.

[§](https://docs.rs#crate-features)Crate Features

| Feature | Default? | Also Enables | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `std` | Y | `alloc` | Use `std`library. |
| `alloc` | Y | Use `alloc`. Enables[wrapping](https://docs.rs#wrapping). | |
| `detect-tty` | N | `std` | See [optional conditions](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#built-in-conditions). |
| `detect-env` | N | `std` | See [optional conditions](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#built-in-conditions). |
| `hyperlink` | N | `std` | Enables [hyperlinking](https://docs.rs/hyperlink/index.html)support. |

With `default-features = false`, this crate is `#[no_std]`.

Without any features enabled, all functionality except [wrapping](https://docs.rs#wrapping) is
available. To recover wrapping *with* `#[no_std]`, set `default-features = false` and enable the `alloc` feature, which requires `alloc` support.

# is-terminal 0.4.17 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/is-terminal/^0.4.11

As of Rust 1.70, most users should use the [ IsTerminal](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/io/trait.IsTerminal.html) trait in the Rust
standard library instead of this crate.

On Unix platforms, this crate now uses libc, so that the implementation
matches what's in std. Users wishing to use the rustix-based implementation
can use the [rustix-is-terminal](https://crates.io/crates/rustix-is-terminal) crate instead.

is-terminal is a simple utility that answers one question:

Is this a terminal?

A "terminal", also known as a "tty", is an I/O device which may be interactive and may support color and other special features. This crate doesn't provide any of those features; it just answers this one question.

On Unix-family platforms, this is effectively the same as the [ isatty](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/isatty.3.html)
function for testing whether a given stream is a terminal, though it accepts
high-level stream types instead of raw file descriptors.

On Windows, it uses a variety of techniques to determine whether the given stream is a terminal.

This crate is derived from [the atty crate](https://crates.io/crates/atty) with [PR #51](https://github.com/softprops/atty/pull/51) bug fix and
[PR #54](https://github.com/softprops/atty/pull/54) port to windows-sys applied. The only additional difference is that
the atty crate only accepts stdin, stdout, or stderr, while this crate accepts
any stream. In particular, this crate does not access any stream that is not
passed to it, in accordance with [I/O safety](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/3128-io-safety.md).

## Example

```
use IsTerminal;
```
## Testing

To test it on a platform manually, use the provided `stdio` example program.
When run normally, it prints this:

```

## Features

Why *y*et another *ANSI* terminal coloring library? Here are some reasons:

- This library makes simple things *simple*:`use``Paint`
- Zero dependencies by default. It really is simple.
- Zero allocations except as needed by opt-in [wrapping](https://docs.rs/yansi/1.0.0/yansi/#wrapping).
- [Automatic Windows support](https://docs.rs/yansi/1.0.0/yansi/#windows)for the vast majority (95%+) of Windows users.
- [Featureful](https://docs.rs/yansi/1.0.0/yansi/#crate-features), no-- `no_std`- `alloc`, support with- `default-features = false`.
- `Style`constructors are- `const`
- *Any*type implementing a formatting trait can be styled, not just strings.
- Styling can be [enabled](https://docs.rs/yansi/1.0.0/yansi/fn.enable.html)and[disabled](https://docs.rs/yansi/1.0.0/yansi/fn.disable.html)globally and[dynamically](https://docs.rs/yansi/1.0.0/yansi/fn.whenever.html), on the fly.
- A `Style`can be predicated on arbitrary[conditions](https://docs.rs/yansi/1.0.0/yansi/#per-style).
- Formatting specifiers like `{:x}`and`{:08b}`are supported and preserved!
- [Built-in (optional) conditions](https://docs.rs/yansi/1.0.0/yansi/struct.Condition.html#built-in-conditions)for- [TTY detection](https://docs.rs/yansi/1.0.0/yansi/struct.Condition.html#impl-Condition-1)and- [common environment variables](https://docs.rs/yansi/1.0.0/yansi/struct.Condition.html#impl-Condition-2).
- Arbitrary items can be *masked*
- Styling can *wrap*
- Styling can *linger*
- Experimental support for [hyperlinking](https://docs.rs/yansi/1.0.0/yansi/hyperlink/index.html)is included.
- The name `yansi`is pretty cool 😎.

- [Built-in (optional) conditions](https://docs.rs/yansi/1.0.0-beta/yansi/struct.Condition.html#built-in-conditions)for- [TTY detection](https://docs.rs/yansi/1.0.0-beta/yansi/struct.Condition.html#impl-Condition-1)and- [common environment variables](https://docs.rs/yansi/1.0.0-beta/yansi/struct.Condition.html#impl-Condition-2).
- Arbitrary items can be *masked*
- Styling can *wrap*
- Experimental support for [hyperlinking](https://docs.rs/yansi/1.0.0-beta/yansi/hyperlink/index.html)is included.
- The name `yansi`is pretty cool 😎.
